name: Ketosis

agents.name: Negative energy balance
agents.notes: The proximate cause. In early lactation, energy demand for milk production exceeds energy intake, and the cow mobilises body fat. The liver cannot fully oxidise the resulting free fatty acids, which are converted to ketone bodies — acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetone — that accumulate in blood, urine and milk.

agents.name: Rumen environment and feed intake
agents.notes: Poor feed quality, sudden dietary change and reduced rumen health reduce energy intake and precipitate the disorder, as does overconditioning at calving, which increases the mobilisation of fat.

hosts.notes: Dairy cows in early lactation are the classic group. Ewes carrying multiple lambs are at risk in the last 6 weeks of pregnancy when the growing fetuses compete with the ewe for glucose. Overconditioned cows are at higher risk than thin ones.

notifiable.note: A production disease with no public health significance. Human ketosis is a separate physiological state and is unrelated to bovine ketosis.

distribution: Worldwide in dairy production, with the highest incidence in intensive systems where cows are fed high-concentrate diets and are selected for very high milk yield. In southern Africa, ketosis is recognised in intensive dairy herds and in ewes in extensive flocks during late pregnancy.

aetiology.summary: Ketosis is a disease of energy imbalance. The cow's energy requirement rises steeply at calving and peaks in early lactation, while feed intake lags behind — the result is a period of negative energy balance in which body fat is mobilised faster than it can be oxidised, and ketone bodies accumulate.
determinants: An energy requirement that exceeds intake, peaking around 2-6 weeks after calving
Impaired adaptation to negative energy balance, with excessive fat mobilisation
Insufficient or unpalatable feed, particularly inadequate concentrate in early lactation
Overconditioning at calving, which increases the amount of fat that can be mobilised
Concurrent conditions — retained placenta, metritis and displaced abomasum all reduce intake and precipitate ketosis
risk_factors: High-producing dairy cows in early lactation
Older cows and those carrying multiple fetuses in sheep
Overconditioned body condition score at calving
Poor transition management and abrupt dietary change
Concurrent disease such as metritis, mastitis or lameness
Hot weather and heat stress reducing intake
In sheep, late pregnancy in ewes carrying twins or triplets
aetiology.epidemiology: Ketosis is most common in the first 4-6 weeks after calving and affects a significant proportion of cows in some herds. It is often subclinical, with only reduced milk yield and fertility as consequences, which makes the true incidence hard to measure. It clusters in herds with poor transition management and in cows with concurrent periparturient disease.

pathophysiology.summary: In negative energy balance, adipose tissue is broken down faster than the liver can process free fatty acids. The liver esterifies excess fatty acids into triglycerides, partly stored and partly exported as very low-density lipoprotein, and the remainder is converted to ketone bodies. When ketone production outpaces utilisation, they accumulate and produce the clinical syndrome, while liver fat accumulation impairs hepatic function.

cascade.title: Negative energy balance
cascade.detail: At calving, energy demand for colostrum and milk synthesis rises abruptly, while dry matter intake falls. The gap is met by mobilising body fat, initially an appropriate adaptation.

cascade.title: Lipid mobilisation and hepatic uptake
cascade.detail: Free fatty acids are released into the circulation and taken up by the liver. When the supply exceeds the liver's capacity for oxidation and export, they are esterified to triglycerides.

cascade.title: Ketone body production
cascade.detail: Excess acetyl-CoA is converted to ketone bodies, which accumulate in the blood and are excreted in milk and urine. Ketones at high concentrations depress appetite, creating a vicious cycle of worsening negative energy balance.

cascade.title: Hepatic lipidosis
cascade.detail: Accumulated triglycerides produce fatty liver, which impairs gluconeogenesis and further reduces the liver's capacity to process the incoming fatty acid load. This is why ketosis and fatty liver are usually described together.

cascade.title: Production loss and clinical signs
cascade.detail: The combination of reduced feed intake, impaired rumen function, liver dysfunction and dehydration produces the clinical picture of a dull, anorexic cow with a rapid drop in milk yield. In sheep, the fetuses continue to demand glucose, and the ewe may progress to recumbency and death.

lesions: Pale, swollen and greasy liver with a fatty, yellow appearance
Increased liver weight with rounded margins
No other specific lesion — diagnosis is primarily clinical and biochemical
Possible evidence of concurrent periparturient disease
clinical_signs: Reduced appetite and reduced feed intake, often with refusal of concentrate
Sharp drop in milk yield, particularly in a high-producing cow
A sweet, acetone-like odour on the breath and in the milk
Hard, dry faeces and reduced rumen motility
In ewes: recumbency, blindness, tremors and eventual death
Subclinical cases show only reduced fertility and reduced milk yield

antemortem: Clinical signs and history of early lactation with reduced appetite and milk yield
Urine dipstick for ketones — a rapid field test with good sensitivity
Milk ketone testing, which is useful for herd-level monitoring
Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate measurement, with concentrations above 1.2 millimoles per litre considered indicative
postmortem: Examine the liver for fatty infiltration, pallor and greasiness
Look for evidence of concurrent disease that precipitated the episode
laboratory: Liver biopsy or post-mortem histology showing fatty change, if required
differentials: Milk fever — recumbency and a response to calcium, not to glucose and ketone management
Displaced abomasum — reduced appetite and milk yield with a characteristic resonant ping
Retained placenta and metritis — fever and vaginal discharge
Rumen acidosis — a different history of concentrate feeding and rumen pH change
Fatty liver disease — usually occurs alongside ketosis rather than as an alternative
In ewes, pregnancy toxaemia is the same pathophysiology and is treated the same way

prevention: Improve transition-cow management, with a properly formulated close-up diet
Avoid overconditioning at calving — aim for a body condition score of about 3.0-3.5
Provide adequate, palatable feed in early lactation and increase concentrate gradually
Monitor early-lactation cows with regular ketone testing of milk or urine
Prevent and treat concurrent periparturient disease promptly
In ewes, feed a balanced diet in late pregnancy and manage litter size stress
control.vaccination: Not applicable — no vaccine exists for a metabolic disorder.
treatment: Intravenous glucose (usually as a 40-50% dextrose solution) corrects hypoglycaemia and is immediately effective but short-lived
Oral propylene glycol or glycerol provides a sustained glucose precursor and is the mainstay of treatment
Corticosteroids such as dexamethasone mobilise glucose and stimulate appetite, but they are contraindicated in late pregnancy and in animals with concurrent infection
Supportive care: encourage feed intake, provide palatable forage and good-quality hay
In ewes, consider a caesarean section or induction of parturition in severe pregnancy toxaemia, alongside glucose therapy
outbreak: Review the transition diet and the body condition of the affected group
Institution of ketone monitoring in early lactation
Identify and address concurrent disease such as metritis or lameness
Adjust the ration to improve energy density and intake in the first weeks of lactation
In sheep flocks, review the late-pregnancy feeding programme for ewes carrying multiples
public_health: Ketosis has no human health significance
Observe milk withdrawal periods for any corticosteroids or other veterinary medicines used
control.notes: Subclinical ketosis is the economically larger problem. A cow does not need to be visibly ill to lose milk yield and fertility — regular monitoring of early-lactation cows catches it before clinical disease.

prognosis: Good with prompt treatment — most cows respond to glucose and propylene glycol within 24-48 hours. Guarded if secondary complications develop or if recumbency has occurred. In ewes, pregnancy toxaemia carries a high mortality without early intervention.
